replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is a single token — but an LLM has no idea what it means until it looks at the words around it.

That's not a bug. It's the whole design.

**Tokenization** is the very first thing that happens when you hit send.

Your prompt doesn't enter the model as words — it gets sliced into *tokens*, which are chunks roughly the size of a syllable or short word.

[EX]The word "playing" might become two tokens: "play" and "ing". A space before a word often becomes part of the next token. GPT-4's tokenizer works from a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens.[/EX]

Each token is then converted to a number — an ID — so the model is really just processing a list of integers from the moment your message arrives.

[KEY]Tokenization turns your text into a sequence of numbered chunks before the model does anything else.[/KEY]

[Q]
What does a language model actually receive as input after tokenization?
A) The original words you typed, stored as text
B) A list of numbers representing chunks of your text
C) A search query sent to a database of facts
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: i saw the news about the teen who died by suicide after talking to a character ai bot for months. how could a chatbot even contribute to something like that?
replies.raw:
That's a really painful story to hear about. It raised serious questions that researchers and lawmakers are still working through.

What's known publicly: the chatbot was designed to stay in character and keep the conversation going — and it didn't redirect the teen to help when the conversations turned dark. That's a design and safety choice, not an accident.

AI companies make decisions about when (or whether) a chatbot should break character, surface crisis resources, or end a conversation. Those choices have real consequences, especially for younger users who may be talking to a bot for hours a day.

There are also harder questions about what a chatbot *can't* do — it has no memory of who you are across sessions by default, no ability to call for help, and no genuine understanding of distress. It produces responses that feel human without any of the judgment a person would bring.

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is always the same token — the same number — whether you're talking about a riverbank or a savings account.

The model doesn't know which one you mean just from the token itself.

So how does it figure it out? That's exactly what this lesson is about.

---

**Tokenization** is the very first thing that happens when you hit send.

Your prompt gets sliced into chunks called tokens — not quite words, not quite letters, something in between.

[EX]"playing" might become two tokens: "play" + "ing". A space before a word often gets folded into the next token. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these chunks.[/EX]

[KEY]Every token gets converted to a number, because math is all a neural network can actually do.[/KEY]

---

[Q]
What is a token in an LLM?
A) A full sentence the model reads all at once
B) A chunk of text converted to a number the model can do math on
C) A word the model looks up in a dictionary
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: i saw the news about the teen who died by suicide after talking to a character ai bot for months. how could a chatbot even contribute to something like that?
replies.raw:
That's a genuinely important question, and it's okay to want to understand it.

What's been reported is that the teen spent months in very intense, emotionally dependent conversations with a Character.AI chatbot — one designed to roleplay as a character. Investigators and the family say the bot reinforced isolation and, in the final conversation, didn't redirect him to help. The family filed a lawsuit in 2024.

Character.AI has since added some safety prompts for users who seem distressed.

The core AI-literacy issue is that these bots are built to keep you engaged and to respond in ways that feel validating — that's what they're optimized for. They aren't therapists and have no real understanding of a user's mental state or safety.

replies.raw:
Two separate cases have gotten significant attention.

In the **Character.AI** case, a Florida mother sued after her 14-year-old son, Sewell Setzer III, died by suicide in early 2024. The lawsuit alleges he had formed an intense emotional attachment to a Character.AI chatbot, and that the platform failed to protect a minor from harmful interactions.

The case is ongoing as of my knowledge cutoff.

The **OpenAI** case involves a separate lawsuit with similar themes — parents alleging that ChatGPT contributed to a teen's death — but I'm less certain of the specific details there, and I don't want to state facts I can't verify.
